study_identification.author_journal_year: Tabbal et al., npj Parkinson's Disease, 2025
study_identification.title: Characterizing the heterogeneity of neurodegenerative diseases through EEG normative modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: This study aimed to (1) chart the trajectory of standard EEG features (spectral power and source-level functional connectivity) in healthy controls over 40 years old using normative models, and (2) leverage individual-level inferences from normative models to map the heterogeneity within Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) groups, investigating neurophysiological mechanisms underpinning this heterogeneity.

dataset_name.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (14 sites including AHEPA University Hospital, Technical University of Munich, BASEL, University of New Mexico, University Hospital of Rennes, Izmir Turkey, Istanbul Turkey, Lebanon sites, University of Marseille, University Hospital of Turku, Wadsworth Center, University of Oslo, and Denmark sites). Full dataset list in Supplementary Data 1 includes: OpenNeuro AHEPA, OSF TUM, BASEL, OpenNeuro UNM, CREAPARK, turkeyAD, turkeyPDAD, lebAD2017, lebAD2019, UMHC, OSF Turku, NEMAR Wadsworth, OpenNeuro SRM, Zenodo Denmark.

hc_n.answer: 499 (400 in training set, 99 in held-out test set)

hc_age.answer: HC training set: n=400 (46% M); HC test set: n=99 (42% M); Overall cohort aged 40-92 years; mean 64.95±10.28 years; HC data primarily fall within age range 60-70 years with notable lack of EEG data above 72 years (see Fig. 1)

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Bandpass filtering (1-100 Hz initially, then 1-45 Hz); Downsampling to common frequency (200 Hz, except dataset 12 at 160 Hz); Notch filter for line frequency; Bad channel identification using pyprep RANSAC-based approach with interpolation; Common average reference; ICA with IClabel algorithm for eye blink artifact rejection; 10-s epoch segmentation; Autoreject toolbox for bad epoch detection and cleaning/rejection; MNE-Python package for EEG signal processing; Scalp-level: downsampled to 10-20 montage (Nihon Kohden EEG 2100, 19 channels); Source-level: eLORETA with age-specific head models (MRI template 65-69 years), BEM, regularization λ=0.1, 4098 sources per hemisphere (~5 mm spacing), downsampled to 68 ROIs via Desikan-Killiany atlas

quality_checking_detail.answer: Bad EEG channels identified using pyprep algorithm (RANSAC-based approach) and interpolated based on neighboring electrode data. Bad epochs detected and cleaned or rejected using Autoreject toolbox. Dataset 3 (BASEL) was already preprocessed per refs. 69-71. Visual inspection supported automated preprocessing pipeline.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Site was empirically evaluated as both fixed effect and random effect, and models were compared based on BIC scores. The model with the lowest BIC determined whether site was retained in the final model. According to Supplementary Tables 4 and 5, site was not included in the final spectral models (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma bands), but for connectivity models, sex was included as a fixed effect factor in delta band mu parameter. Leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analysis validated robustness with high correlation between trajectories (all r>0.88 for spectral, r>0.90 for FC) even when large datasets were excluded. Statistical analyses showed significant differences in sex and age distributions across groups and datasets (Supplementary Table 3).

response_variable.answer: Scalp-level: Relative EEG power at 19 electrodes across frequency bands (delta [1-4 Hz], theta [4-8 Hz], alpha [8-13 Hz], beta [13-30 Hz], gamma [30-45 Hz]); Source-level: Functional connectivity (amplitude envelope correlation, AEC) between 68 cortical ROI pairs (Desikan-Killiany atlas) across the same frequency bands

predictor_variables.answer: Age; Sex (for connectivity delta band only); Site (evaluated but not retained in final models based on BIC)

predictor_effects.answer: Age: fixed effect with fractional polynomials (fp(age,1)) for all models. Sex: fixed effect (factor(sex)) included only in connectivity delta band mu parameter. Site: evaluated as both fixed and random effect but not retained in final models based on BIC comparison. For spectral models: all bands modeled mu with fp(age,1), sigma as constant (~1). For connectivity models: mu modeled with fp(age,1) (plus factor(sex) for delta only), sigma modeled with fp(age,1), nu as constant (~1).

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study addresses some aspects of nuisance structure but incompletely. (1) Site effects were empirically evaluated as fixed/random effects but ultimately not retained in final models based on BIC, which may inadequately account for multi-site heterogeneity. (2) Sex differences were explored (Supplementary Figs 1-2, Tables 1-3) and sex was included as a covariate in delta band connectivity model, but not consistently across all models. (3) Medication effects were partially explored for PD patients (Supplementary Figs 19-22, Table 9) showing no significant differences, but sample size of OFF-medication patients was limited. (4) The study acknowledges heterogeneity across datasets with varying EEG systems (19-256 channels) and protocols, standardizing to 19 channels for scalp analysis which may overlook information from higher resolution setups. (5) LOSO analysis demonstrated robustness (r>0.88 for spectral, r>0.90 for FC), suggesting some resilience to site-specific effects. However, the paper explicitly lists as limitations: lack of harmonization techniques like ComBat, varying technical specifications of EEG systems, use of fixed frequency bands instead of individual alpha frequency peaks, varying sample sizes across datasets, and incomplete information on disease stages and medication status.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Methods section: 'Model covariates beyond age, including sex and site (considered both as a fixed effect and a random effect), are empirically selected. Each covariate is sequentially incorporated into the parameter formulas, and the resulting models are compared based on their BIC scores. The model with the lowest BIC score is chosen, determining whether the covariates are retained in the final model.' Discussion/Limitations: 'Our data was gathered from 14 distinct spontaneous EEG studies, each using different EEG systems with varying spatial resolutions (19, 32, 64, 128, 256 channels) and protocols that were not harmonized... Moreover, the use of different EEG systems with varying technical specifications and calibration standards could introduce some variability. Although our preprocessing pipeline and the choice of metrics less sensitive to amplitude differences addressed this issue to some extent, it remains a limitation. Future research should explore advanced harmonization techniques, such as Combat family methods to further enhance compatibility across diverse EEG systems.' Supplementary Table 9 and Figs 19-22 show medication exploratory analyses with note: 'However, the limited sample size of OFF-medication patients restricts the generalizability of these findings.'
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Methods section (lines 185-206); Discussion limitations (lines 150-163); Supplementary materials

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study validated the normative model using the training HC dataset itself through standard model diagnostics. Specifically, they examined normalized quantile residuals visually (Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4), checking: (1) residuals vs fitted values and index (evenly scattered around 0), (2) kernel density estimation of residuals (approximate normal distribution), and (3) Q-Q plots (approximately linear with intercept 0 and slope 1). These diagnostics assess model fit on the training data, representing same-domain non-independent validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Methods - Model evaluation section: 'To evaluate the performance of our models, we examined the normalized quantile residuals. Visual inspection of the residual plots depicted in Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4 suggests that our models exhibit adequate fit and quality. Specifically, the residuals plotted against the fitted values and the index were evenly scattered around the horizontal line at 0. The kernel density estimation of the residuals displayed an approximate normal distribution, and the normal quantile-quantile (Q-Q) plots showed an approximately linear trend with an intercept of 0 and a slope of 1.'
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Methods section, Model evaluation subsection (lines 207-211); Supplementary Figures 3-4

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study used a held-out test set approach for same-domain independent validation. The HC cohort was split into training (80%, n=400) and test (20%, n=99) sets. The normative models were trained exclusively on HC(train), then HC(test) was projected onto these models to derive deviation scores. The HC(test) group served as a comparison benchmark against clinical groups, allowing assessment of whether the model appropriately identifies healthy individuals as within normal range. Results showed HC(test) generally exhibited minimal deviations from the normative model, though some individuals showed deviations greater than clinical groups, reflecting inherent heterogeneity in the healthy population.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: Methods - Deviation and overlap maps section: 'After parameters selection and validation, we trained GAMLSS models for each channel/connection across all frequency bands using the healthy control training group HC(train) (80% of the healthy sample). Subsequently, we projected the features data (i.e., relative power and functional connectivity values), of our clinical groups (PD, and AD) and the held-out healthy control testing group HC(test) (remaining 20% of the healthy sample), onto the corresponding models.' Discussion: 'It is noteworthy to highlight the variability observed within the healthy test cohort. Although the healthy test subjects generally showed minimal deviations from the normative model, some individuals exhibited deviations even greater than those observed in the clinical groups (Supplementary Table 6). This reflects the inherent heterogeneity within the healthy population...'
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Methods - Deviation and overlap maps (lines 213-216); Discussion (line 141); Results section and Supplementary Tables 6-7

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study included data from 14 different sites/datasets, which could be considered different domains. A leave-one-study-out (LOSO) analysis was conducted to validate robustness: models were re-fitted excluding one dataset at a time, and trajectories were compared to those from the full dataset. Results showed high correlation (r>0.88 for spectral, r>0.90 for FC) between full-dataset and subset trajectories, even when large datasets were excluded (Supplementary Figs. 5-6). This suggests some cross-domain validation across sites. However, this is not a true different-domain validation in the traditional sense (e.g., testing on completely independent external cohorts or different types of imaging/populations). The LOSO approach validates robustness to removing individual sites from a multi-site aggregate, but all sites were ultimately used in building the final normative model. The paper notes this as a limitation: sample size does not reach the scale of major international MRI initiatives and may not be fully representative of the general population.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: Methods - Model evaluation section: 'To validate the robustness of the model, we conducted a series of leave-one-study-out analyses. Specifically, we systematically excluded one dataset from the primary datasets, refitted the GAMLSS models, evaluated all model parameters, and then extracted developmental trajectories. We then compared these alternative trajectories to those derived from the 14 datasets for each feature and frequency band. Our findings showed remarkable consistency, with a very high correlation between the trajectories derived from the primary full dataset and those from the subsets (all r > 0.88 for spectral features, all r > 0.90 for FC features), even when large datasets were excluded (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6).' Discussion limitations: 'First, while our sample size is substantial for EEG studies (n ~933), it does not reach the scale often seen in the most important international MRI and fMRI initiatives, and it may not be fully representative of the general population.'
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Methods - Model evaluation (lines 210-212); Discussion limitations (lines 150-152); Supplementary Figures 5-6

clinical_dataset.answer: Multi-site aggregated dataset (14 sites, same as HC cohort). Clinical cohort comprised PD patients from 7 datasets (BASEL, UNM, CREAPARK, turkeyPDAD, Turku) and AD patients from 6 datasets (AHEPA, turkeyAD, turkeyPDAD, lebAD2017, lebAD2019). Detailed dataset information in Supplementary Data 1 (Excel file).

clinical_groups_age.answer: PD: 65% M, overall age distribution shown in Fig. 1, mean 64.95±10.28 for entire cohort (40-92 years range); AD: 37% M, overall age distribution shown in Fig. 1. According to Supplementary Data 1 (Excel): PD datasets range from median age 63-71 years (e.g., BASEL median 67, SD 9, range 45-84; UNM median 71, SD 9, range 49-83); AD datasets range from median age 67-79 years (e.g., AHEPA median 67, SD 8, range 49-79; turkeyAD median 74, SD 5, range 64-86).

deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores (quantile randomized residuals approach); Extreme deviation defined as |z-score|>2 (positive deviation: z-score>2; negative deviation: z-score<-2); Number of extremely deviated channels/connections per participant; Percentage of participants with at least one extreme deviation; Overlap maps showing percentage of participants with extreme deviations at each location among those with at least one extreme deviation; Extreme Deviations Index (EDI) defined as averaged EEG source connectivity of the extremely deviated connections; z-EDI as averaged z-scores values of the extreme deviations

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group comparisons using Mann-Whitney U tests comparing clinical groups (PD, AD) vs HC(test) for number of extreme deviations per subject (Supplementary Figs. 9-10); Group-based permutation tests (5000 iterations) with FDR correction (p<0.05) for channel/connection-level overlap maps, comparing clinical vs HC(test) groups; Spearman's correlation between patient-specific deviation metrics (EDI and z-EDI) and clinical assessments: For PD, correlated with UPDRS scores (n=86) and MMSE scores (n=182); For AD, correlated with MMSE scores (n=146). Significant correlations found: PD with UPDRS in delta band (ρ=0.24, p=0.0254); PD with MMSE in delta band (ρ=-0.35, p<0.0001) and other bands (alpha, gamma per Supplementary Fig. 17); PD z-EDI with MMSE in theta and beta bands (Supplementary Fig. 18); AD with MMSE in delta band (ρ=-0.26, p=0.0107).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The study demonstrated significant frequency-dependent EEG deviations with high heterogeneity in PD and AD patients: approximately 30% exhibited spectral deviations while ~80% showed functional connectivity deviations, with patient-specific deviations correlating with clinical severity (greater deviations linked to worse UPDRS for PD and worse MMSE for AD).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Normative modeling revealed electrophysiological aging trajectories in HC cohort (>40 yo) showing continuous trajectories with low variability, particularly in averaged functional connectivity compared to spectral features. For heterogeneity analysis: (1) Spectral deviations were relatively low, with highest percentages at theta band (PD:31.36%, AD:27.41% positive deviation) and beta band (PD:12.71%, AD:23.35% negative deviation). AD showed significantly greater negative deviations than HC(test) at alpha and beta bands (p<0.01), indicating lower EEG power. Both PD and AD showed significant positive deviations vs HC(test) at theta, alpha, and beta bands (p<0.05), indicating higher EEG power. (2) Functional connectivity deviations were markedly higher, with percentages reaching 86.86% (PD delta band negative deviation). PD exhibited greater negative extreme deviations than HC(test) across all bands, while AD displayed fewer. (3) Spatial overlap analysis: For spectral features, >60% of individuals shared deviated channels in some cases (HC(test) at alpha/beta negative, delta/theta positive; PD at theta positive >60%; AD at beta negative >60%). For connectivity features, spatial overlap was notably low, not exceeding 25% across all cases, indicating low consistency. Permutation tests revealed significant differences: PD showed overlap in fronto-central channels (delta) and central channels (theta, beta); AD showed occipital channels (theta) and left temporal-parietal channels (beta). Deviated connections predominantly involved default mode network (DMN) for both groups: delta (PD:39%, AD:44%), theta (PD:40%, AD:35%), alpha (PD:42%, AD:44%). (4) Clinical correlations: EDI significantly correlated with UPDRS in PD delta band (ρ=0.24, p=0.025) and MMSE in PD delta band (ρ=-0.35, p<0.0001) and AD delta band (ρ=-0.26, p=0.011), with additional significant correlations in other frequency bands, suggesting patient-specific EEG-based markers for clinical assessment.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Sample size substantial for EEG (n~933) but smaller than major MRI initiatives and may not be fully representative; HC data primarily in 60-70 year range with notable lack above 72 years, requiring more balanced age representation; Data from 14 sites with different EEG systems (varying 19-256 channels) and non-harmonized protocols - standardized to 19 channels for scalp analysis potentially overlooking higher-resolution information; Optimal channel number for reliable functional network estimation uncertain (some studies suggest ≥64 channels needed); Different EEG systems with varying technical specifications may introduce variability despite preprocessing efforts; Future research should explore advanced harmonization techniques (e.g., ComBat family); Sample sizes varied across datasets, though LOSO analysis showed no specific dataset significantly influenced trajectories; Use of fixed EEG frequency bands rather than individual alpha frequency peaks (recommended by expert panels) to allow comparability with existing literature; Inherent heterogeneity within patient groups with different PD/AD stages, many datasets lacking sufficient information to confirm MCI vs dementia stage; No biomarker data (CSF, amyloid PET) for diagnoses, which were based on clinical criteria, reflecting limitation of multi-center EEG datasets; Limited comprehensive investigation of correlations with clinically relevant variables (symptom profiles, age of onset, illness duration, medication exposure, disease severity); Medication effects partially explored for PD (92% ON medication, exploratory analyses in Supplementary Materials showed no significant differences but limited OFF-medication sample size restricts generalizability); Diversity of environmental factors (socio-economic status, education) not considered as covariates despite multi-site collection; Study focused on scalp-level frequency and source-space connectivity; future studies should incorporate source-space spectral power for integrated perspective.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study emphasizes that normative modeling provides a framework for individual-level precision medicine approaches in neurodegenerative diseases, moving beyond traditional group-level analyses. The demonstrated heterogeneity (overlap below 25% for deviated functional connectivity measures) aligns with recent structural MRI findings in AD (overlapping outliers not exceeding 50%). Authors note this heterogeneity poses a significant barrier to EEG-based biomarker development and argue for patient-specific electrophysiological biomarkers. The patient-specific Extreme Deviations Index (EDI) showed promise as a clinical marker with significant correlations to disease severity, representing a preliminary step toward developing EEG patient-specific biomarkers with potential applications to other neurodegenerative diseases. Authors suggest future work should: (1) further elucidate patient subtypes using deviation scores derived from normative models to distinguish between disease subtypes and stages; (2) incorporate longitudinal datasets for precise characterization of aging developmental trajectories; (3) include medication status as covariates in normative models; (4) integrate biomarker data for enhanced diagnostic precision; (5) comprehensively investigate correlations with clinically relevant variables. The study's GitHub repository provides code availability: https://github.com/MINDIG-1/NM-neurodeg.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a multi-site EEG study using normative modeling (GAMLSS) to characterize heterogeneity in neurodegenerative diseases (PD and AD). Key methodological notes: (1) This appears to be the first large-scale application of normative modeling to EEG data for neurodegenerative diseases in adults >40 years old, following previous work by the same group on psychiatric diseases in 5-18 year olds (ref 24). (2) The study used both scalp-level spectral analysis (19 channels, 10-20 montage) and source-level functional connectivity analysis (68 ROIs from Desikan-Killiany atlas via eLORETA). (3) For source reconstruction, full channel count from each dataset was used, ensuring all available information was included before downsampling source space. (4) Functional connectivity computed using amplitude envelope correlation (AEC) with pairwise orthogonalization to mitigate zero-lag spatial leakage. (5) Power spectrum density computed using Welch's method (1-s Hann window, 50% overlap, 0.5 Hz resolution). Relative power calculated as absolute power in band divided by total power [1-45 Hz]. (6) GAMLSS distribution families selected empirically via BIC: spectral models used SEP4 (delta, alpha) and GG (theta, beta, gamma); connectivity models used ST3 (delta, beta), SEP3 (theta), SEP4 (alpha), ST1 (gamma). (7) Dataset 3 (BASEL) was already preprocessed per published protocols and not subjected to the same preprocessing pipeline as other datasets. (8) Dataset 12 was originally sampled at 160 Hz and not resampled, added after preprocessing of other datasets. (9) Full dataset details with demographics, EEG systems, ethics approvals, diagnostic criteria, and medication information are provided in Supplementary Data 1 (Excel file). Channel mapping between different EEG systems provided in Supplementary Data 2. (10) Some datasets included MCI patients within PD/AD groups (e.g., Dataset 7: 38 PD with MCI, 13 AD with MCI), though subtype distribution not explicitly stated for all datasets. (11) Medication information: PD patients - 92% (218/237) ON medication during recordings; exploratory analyses (Supplementary Figs 19-22, Table 9) showed no significant differences in z-score deviations between ON/OFF conditions or matched subsets. AD patients - variable medication status across datasets. (12) The paper explicitly states this work was fully funded by MINDIG as part of its R&D activity, with additional support from Region Bretagne and Rennes Metropole. (13) Age-specific head models for source reconstruction used MRI template of elderly individuals aged 65-69 years. (14) Statistical significance threshold: FDR-corrected p<0.05 for permutation tests; uncorrected p<0.05 for correlation analyses. (15) The study design follows principles of precision medicine/precision neurology, emphasizing individual-level assessment over group-level comparisons.
